categories.title: Arabic Alphabet
categories.description: The 28 letters, their forms, positions, and characteristics — the foundation of Arabic reading and writing

children.title: Introduction to the Arabic Alphabet
children.description: Arabic is written right-to-left with 28 letters. Each letter has a name, a sound, and a shape that changes based on position in a word. The script is cursive — letters in a word usually connect.
children.example: ا ب ت ث ج ح خ د ذ ر ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ع غ ف ق ك ل م ن ه و ي
children.exampleTranslation: The 28 letters in the classical order

children.title: The Classical Order (الترتيب الهجائي)
children.description: The 28 letters are traditionally ordered by similarity of shape and sound. This is the standard order used in schools and dictionaries.
children.example: أ ب ت ث ج ح خ د ذ ر ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ع غ ف ق ك ل م ن ه و ي
children.exampleTranslation: The abjad-hawwaz order used in modern teaching

children.title: The Abjad Order (الترتيب الأبجدي)
children.description: An older ordering used for numerology and historical texts. Groups letters into eight mnemonic words: أَبْجَد هَوَّز حُطِّي كَلَمُن سَعْفَص قَرَشَت ثَخَذ ضَظَغ.
children.example: أ ب ج د ه و ز ح ط ي ك ل م ن س ع ف ص ق ر ش ت ث خ ذ ض ظ غ
children.exampleTranslation: The Abjad numeral order (used for numbers before Islam)

children.title: 28 Letters — But 29 Sounds
children.description: There are 28 letters, but the Hamza (ء) is treated as a separate sound. Some scholars count it as a distinct letter, bringing the total to 29.
children.example: الهمزة ليست حرفاً في العدّ المشهور
children.exampleTranslation: Hamza is not counted as a letter in the standard count

children.title: No Uppercase or Lowercase
children.description: Unlike Latin script, Arabic letters have no uppercase/lowercase distinction. However, they do change shape based on position (isolated, initial, medial, final).

children.title: Ligatures (التراكيب)
children.description: Some letter combinations form special ligatures. The most famous is ل + ا = لا (lā). Others include الله (Allah) which is often written as a single glyph.

children.title: The Four Forms of Each Letter
children.description: Most letters change shape depending on whether they are at the beginning, middle, or end of a word, or standing alone.

children.title: Isolated Form (منفصل)
children.description: The letter standing alone, not connected to any other letter.

children.title: Initial Form (أول الكلمة)
children.description: The letter at the beginning of a word. It connects to the following letter.

children.title: Medial Form (وسط الكلمة)
children.description: The letter in the middle of a word. It connects on both sides.

children.title: Final Form (آخر الكلمة)
children.description: The letter at the end of a word. It connects to the preceding letter only.

children.title: Complete Forms Table
children.description: All 28 letters with their four forms and names.
children.example: ب: بـ ـبـ ـب / ت: تـ ـتـ ـت / ث: ثـ ـثـ ـث ...

children.title: ا (Alif) — لا يتصل
children.description: Alif connects to the preceding letter only. Never to the following. Forms: ا (isolated), ـا (final).
children.exampleTranslation: Alif never has initial or medial form

children.title: د (Dāl) — لا يتصل
children.description: Dāl connects to the preceding letter only. Forms: د، ـد.

children.title: The Six Non-Connecting Letters
children.description: Six letters never connect to the following letter, even in the middle of a word. They only connect to the letter before them.
children.example: ا د ذ ر ز و
children.exampleTranslation: Alif, Dāl, Dhāl, Rāʾ, Zāy, Wāw

children.title: ا (Alif)
children.description: Never connects forward. Always has a fixed shape.
children.exampleTranslation: Bāb — Alif is at the end

children.title: د (Dāl)
children.description: Only connects to the previous letter.
children.exampleTranslation: Dār — Dāl has no forward connection

children.title: ذ (Dhāl)
children.description: Only connects to the previous letter.

children.title: ر (Rāʾ)
children.description: Only connects to the previous letter.

children.title: ز (Zāy)
children.description: Only connects to the previous letter.

children.title: و (Wāw)
children.description: Only connects to the previous letter.

children.title: Sun and Moon Letters
children.description: When the definite article ال is prefixed to a word, the Lām is either pronounced (moon letters) or silent with the following letter doubled (sun letters).

children.title: Sun Letters (الحروف الشمسية) — 14 Letters
children.description: After a sun letter, the Lām of ال is silent and the sun letter takes a Shaddah. Sun letters: ت ث د ذ ر ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ل ن.
children.example: الشَّمْس، النَّهْر، الدَّرْس، الرَّحْمَن، الزَّيْت، السَّمَاء، الصَّلَاة، الطَّعَام، الظُّلْم، اللَّيْل، النُّور

children.title: Moon Letters (الحروف القمرية) — 14 Letters
children.description: After a moon letter, the Lām of ال is pronounced with Sukūn. Moon letters: أ ب ج ح خ ع غ ف ق ك م ه و ي.
children.example: الْقَمَر، الْبَاب، الْجَبَل، الْحَقّ، الْخَيْر، الْعِلْم، الْغَيْب، الْفَجْر، الْكِتَاب، الْمَاء، الْهُدَى، الْوَلَد، الْيَوْم
children.exampleTranslation: Moon letter examples with silent Lām

children.title: Mnemonic for Sun Letters
children.description: The 14 sun letters collected in: طِبْ ثُمَّ صِلْ رَحِمًا تَفُزْ ضِفْ ذَا نِعَمْ / دَعْ سُوءَ ظَنٍّ زُرْ شَرِيفًا لِلْكَرَمْ.
children.example: ط ث ص ر ت ض ذ ن د س ظ ز ش ل

children.title: Similar Letters (Easily Confused)
children.description: Groups of letters that look or sound alike and are often confused by beginners. Learning to distinguish them is essential.
children.example: ب ت ث / ج ح خ / د ذ / ر ز

children.title: ب ت ث — Same Base, Different Dots
children.description: All three share the same base shape. Dots differ: ب (1 below), ت (2 above), ث (3 above).

children.title: ج ح خ — Same Base, Different Dots
children.description: ج (dot inside), ح (no dot), خ (dot above).

children.title: د ذ — Same Base, Different Dots
ر ز — Same Base, Different Dots
س ش — Same Base, Different Dots
ص ض — Same Base, Different Dots
children.description: ص (no dot), ض (dot above). Also emphatic versions of س and د.

children.title: ط ظ — Same Base, Different Dots
children.description: ط (no dot), ظ (dot above). Emphatic versions of ت and ذ.

children.title: ع غ — Same Base, Different Dots
ف ق — Same Shape, Different Dots
children.description: ف (1 dot above), ق (2 dots above).

children.title: ح خ ه ة — Ḥāʾ Family Confusion
children.description: Beginners often confuse ح, خ, ه, and ة. They have different Makhārij (articulation points) and different sounds.

children.title: ا vs أ إ آ ء — Alif vs Hamza
children.description: ا is a long vowel; أ إ آ are hamza carrying different vowels; ء is standalone hamza. Very common confusion point.

children.title: Hamza — Complete Guide
children.description: Hamza is not counted as one of the 28 letters but is a distinct sound. It can appear standalone or on a carrier letter (ا، و، ي).
children.example: أ إ آ ؤ ئ ء
children.exampleTranslation: The six written forms of hamza

children.title: The Six Written Forms
children.description: Hamza appears as: أ (on alif with fatḥah/ḍammah), إ (on alif with kasrah), آ (maddah — alif + hamza), ؤ (on wāw), ئ (on yā), ء (standalone).
children.example: أَخ / إِبْرَاهِيم / آمَنَ / مُؤْمِن / بِئْر / شَيْء

children.title: Hamzat al-Waṣl vs Hamzat al-Qaṭʿ
children.description: Hamzat al-Waṣl (ا without hamza mark) is silent when continuing. Hamzat al-Qaṭʿ (أ) is always pronounced.
children.exampleTranslation: Waṣl is silent in continuation; Qaṭʿ is always heard

children.title: Hamza at Word Beginning
children.description: Always pronounced, whether the word stands alone or is connected. Examples: أَب، إِبْن، أُمّ.

children.title: Hamza in the Middle
children.description: Can be on alif, wāw, yā, or standalone depending on the surrounding vowels. Examples: سَأَلَ، مُؤْمِن، بِئْر، مَاء.

children.title: Hamza at Word End
children.description: Usually on a carrier or standalone. Examples: شَيْء، سَمَاء، قُرَّاء.

children.title: Special Letters & Marks
children.description: Additional characters and letter forms used in Arabic writing.

children.title: Tāʾ Marbūṭah (ة)
children.description: A Tāʾ with two dots written in a rounded form. Occurs mostly at the end of feminine nouns and adjectives. Pronounced as 'h' at pause, 't' in construction.

children.title: Alif Maqṣūrah (ى)
children.description: An Alif written as a dotless Yāʾ. Represents a long 'ā' sound. Common in Qur'anic Arabic.

children.title: Lām-Alif Ligature (لا)
children.description: A compulsory ligature combining Lām + Alif. Appears in words like لَا (no).

children.title: ة vs ه — When to Use Which
children.description: ة is a feminine marker at word end; ه is a regular letter pronounced 'h'. Beginners often mix them.

children.title: Basic Pronunciation Guide
children.description: Each letter's closest English approximation. Note that some Arabic sounds have no English equivalent.
children.example: ا = a, ب = b, ت = t ...

children.title: ا (Alif) — 'a' as in 'father'
children.description: Long open 'a'. Not found in English exactly but close to the 'a' in 'father'.

children.title: ت (Tāʾ) — 't' as in 'take'
children.description: Light t, tongue tip at upper teeth.

children.title: ج (Jīm) — 'j' as in 'jam'
children.description: Similar to English j (Egyptian Arabic uses a hard 'g').

children.title: ح (Ḥāʾ) — No English equivalent
children.description: A deep, whispered breath from the middle throat. Distinguish from ه.

children.title: خ (Khāʾ) — 'kh' as in Scottish 'loch'
children.description: A raspy, whispered sound from the nearest throat.

children.title: ر (Rāʾ) — Rolled 'r'
children.description: Similar to Spanish r — a light trill, tongue tip vibrating against gums.

children.title: ص (Ṣād) — Emphatic 's'
children.description: Like English s but with a deeper, heavier sound. Back of tongue raised.

children.title: ض (Ḍād) — Emphatic 'd'
children.description: Unique to Arabic. Heavy d from the tongue edge.

children.title: ع (ʿAyn) — No English equivalent
children.description: A deep constriction at the middle throat. Very common in Arabic.

children.title: ق (Qāf) — Deep 'k'
children.description: Like English k but from the deepest part of the tongue. Distinguish from ك.

children.title: ه (Hāʾ) — 'h' as in 'hat'
children.description: Same as English h. Distinguish from ح.

children.title: و (Wāw) — 'w' as in 'wet'
children.description: Same as English w. Also a long vowel 'ū'.

children.title: ي (Yāʾ) — 'y' as in 'yes'
children.description: Same as English y. Also a long vowel 'ī'.

categories.title: Vowels & Diacritics
categories.description: The short vowels (Ḥarakāt), doubled vowels (Tanween), and additional diacritical marks that control Arabic pronunciation

children.title: Short Vowels (الحركات)
children.description: Three short vowels modify the consonant they sit on.

children.title: Fatḥah (ـَ)
children.description: A small diagonal stroke above a letter. Produces a short 'a' sound.

children.title: Kasrah (ـِ)
children.description: A small diagonal stroke below a letter. Produces a short 'i' sound.

children.title: Ḍammah (ـُ)
children.description: A small curl above a letter. Produces a short 'u' sound.

children.title: Tanween (التنوين)
children.description: Doubled vowel marks at the end of a noun, indicating indefiniteness. Pronounced as -an, -un, -in.

children.title: Tanween Fatḥ (ـًا)
children.description: Doubled Fatḥah, usually written over an added Alif. Pronounced 'an'.

children.title: Sukūn & Shaddah
children.description: Two marks that modify consonants without adding a vowel.

children.title: Sukūn (ـْ)
children.description: A small circle above a letter. Indicates the letter has no vowel.

children.title: Shaddah (ـّ)
children.description: Doubles the letter. The first instance is Sākinah, the second is voweled.

children.title: Shaddah with Vowels
children.description: Shaddah can carry any of the three short vowels or the two Tanween marks.

children.title: Long Vowels (حروف المد)
children.description: The three Madd letters elongate the short vowels into long ones, held for 2 counts.

children.title: Special Diacritical Marks
children.description: Additional marks beyond the basic vowels.

children.title: Dagger Alif (ـٰ)
children.description: A small vertical mark above a letter, representing an omitted Alif. Common in الرَّحْمَٰن.

children.title: Small Wāw (ۥ)
children.description: A tiny Wāw above a letter, indicating a dropped Wāw in pronunciation.

children.title: Small Yāʾ (ۦ)
children.description: A tiny Yāʾ above a letter, indicating a dropped Yāʾ in pronunciation.

children.title: Small Mīm (ۢ)
children.description: A tiny Mīm above a letter, indicating Iqlāb (conversion) of Nūn to Mīm.

children.title: Waqf Signs (علامات الوقف)
children.description: Marks in the Muṣḥaf indicating where to stop or continue: م، ج، لا، قلى، صلى.

children.title: Sajdah Mark (۩)
children.description: A mark in the Muṣḥaf indicating a prostration verse.

children.title: Alif Forms & Variants
children.description: The Alif has several forms depending on position and context.
children.example: ا أ إ آ ى ـا

children.title: Plain Alif (ا)
children.description: Long 'a' vowel or Hamzat al-Waṣl at word start.

children.title: ـا (Alif after Tatweel)
children.description: Alif attached after a Tatweel (ــ) for calligraphy.

children.title: Hamza Seats (كراسي الهمزة)
children.description: When Hamza is not standalone, it sits on a carrier letter: ا، و، ي, depending on the surrounding vowels.

children.title: On Alif (أ إ آ)
children.description: When Hamza has Fatḥah or Ḍammah, or is preceded by one.

children.title: On Wāw (ؤ)
children.description: When Hamza has Ḍammah and the preceding letter has Ḍammah.

children.title: On Yāʾ (ئ)
children.description: When Hamza has Kasrah or is preceded by Kasrah.

children.title: Standalone (ء)
children.description: When Hamza follows a long vowel or Sākinah letter.

children.title: Vowel Assimilation & Elision
children.description: How vowels shift or drop when word forms change.

children.title: What Is Assimilation?
children.description: When vowels or weak letters (و، ي، ا) change or drop during word formation. E.g., قَالَ → قُلْ (imperative).

children.title: Common Examples
children.description: بَاعَ → بِعْ / نَامَ → نَمْ / صَامَ → صُمْ.

children.title: Reading Practice — Voweled Words
children.description: Practice reading words with all vowels and diacritics applied.

children.title: Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah (Al-Fātiḥah 1:1-7)
children.description: Complete Sūrah with all diacritics — the foundation of daily recitation.

categories.title: Nouns, Gender, Number & Definiteness
categories.description: The anatomy of Arabic nouns — types, gender, number, and how definiteness works

children.title: What Is a Noun? (الاسم)
children.description: A noun names a person, place, thing, or idea. Arabic nouns carry gender, number, case, and definiteness information.

children.title: Definition
children.description: An Arabic noun (اسم) is a word that names something — physical, abstract, or conceptual. It can be a person, place, thing, quality, or idea.

children.title: Concrete vs Abstract
children.description: Concrete nouns refer to physical objects; abstract nouns refer to concepts.

children.title: Types of Nouns
children.description: Arabic classifies nouns in several ways: proper vs common, concrete vs abstract, and more.

children.title: Proper Noun (اسم علم)
children.description: A specific name — person, place, book, etc.

children.title: Common Noun (اسم جنس)
children.description: Refers to a class or category.

children.title: Abstract Noun (اسم معنى)
children.description: Refers to a concept or quality.

children.title: Collective Noun (اسم جمع)
children.description: Refers to a group as a single entity.

children.title: Verbal Noun (المصدر)
children.description: The noun form of a verb, similar to English -ing forms but functioning as a noun.

children.title: Diminutive (التصغير)
children.description: A form indicating smallness or affection. Pattern: فُعَيْل or فُعَيْعِل.

children.title: Gender (المذكر والمؤنث)
children.description: Every Arabic noun is either masculine or feminine. The default is masculine; feminine is usually marked.

children.title: Masculine (المذكر)
children.description: The default gender. Any noun without a feminine marker is assumed masculine.

children.title: Feminine (المؤنث)
children.description: Marked by one of three signs: Tāʾ Marbūṭah (ة), Alif Maqṣūrah (ى), or Alif Mamdūdah (اء). Some nouns are feminine without a marker.

children.title: Alif Maqṣūrah (ى)
children.description: Some feminine nouns end in ى.

children.title: Naturally Feminine Without Marker
children.description: Some nouns are feminine by nature even without a marker: أُمّ (mother), أُخْت (sister), بِنْت (daughter), etc.

children.title: Broken Plurals of Inanimate Nouns Are Feminine
children.description: Broken plurals of non-human nouns take feminine singular agreement.
children.exampleTranslation: Al-kutubu jadīdah (the books are new — feminine singular)

children.title: Common Gender (Both)
children.description: A few nouns can be either masculine or feminine depending on usage.

children.title: Number (العدد)
children.description: Arabic has three numbers: singular, dual, and plural.

children.title: Dual (المثنى)
children.description: Exactly two. Formed by adding ـَان (nominative) or ـَيْن (accusative/genitive).

children.title: Plural (الجمع)
children.description: Three or more. Arabic has two types: sound plural (regular) and broken plural (irregular).

children.title: Sound Masculine Plural (جمع مذكر سالم)
children.description: Formed by adding ـُونَ (nom.) or ـِينَ (acc./gen.) to the singular. Used for male humans and some adjectives.

children.title: Sound Feminine Plural (جمع مؤنث سالم)
children.description: Formed by adding ـَات to the singular. Used for female humans, most feminine nouns, and some masculine inanimate nouns.

children.title: Broken Plural (جمع تكسير)
children.description: The singular's pattern is 'broken' or changed. There are many patterns; each noun has its own broken plural.
children.example: كِتَاب → كُتُب / بَيْت → بُيُوت / رَجُل → رِجَال
children.exampleTranslation: Kitāb → kutub / bayt → buyūt / rajul → rijāl

children.title: Common Broken Plural Patterns
children.description: Common patterns: أَفْعَال، فُعُول، فِعَال، أَفْعِلَة، فَوَاعِل.

children.title: Definiteness (المعرفة والنكرة)
children.description: Arabic nouns are either definite (known) or indefinite (unknown). This affects the noun's form and how adjectives agree.

children.title: The Definite Article ال
children.description: Prefixed to a noun to make it definite. Its Lām is pronounced before moon letters and silent (with the following letter doubled) before sun letters.

children.title: The 7 Types of Definite Nouns
children.description: Definite nouns include: 1. Proper nouns. 2. Pronouns. 3. Demonstratives. 4. Relative pronouns. 5. Nouns with ال. 6. Nouns in Iḍāfah with a definite second term. 7. Vocatives.
children.example: مُحَمَّد / هُوَ / هَذَا / الَّذِي / الْكِتَاب / كِتَابُ مُحَمَّدٍ / يَا رَجُلُ

children.title: Indefinite with Tanween
children.description: Indefinite nouns end in Tanween (ً ٌ ٍ). Example: كِتَابٌ / كِتَابًا / كِتَابٍ.

children.title: Case (الإعراب) — Overview
children.description: Arabic nouns change their ending depending on their role in the sentence. There are three cases.

children.title: Nominative (الرفع)
children.description: Default case for subjects. Ending: ـُ or ـٌ (Tanween Ḍamm).

children.title: Accusative (النصب)
children.description: Case for direct objects and other positions. Ending: ـَ or ـًا (Tanween Fatḥ).

children.title: Genitive (الجر)
children.description: Case after prepositions and in possessive constructions. Ending: ـِ or ـٍ (Tanween Kasr).

children.title: Common Noun Errors for Beginners
children.description: Mistakes beginners make when learning Arabic nouns.

children.title: Assuming All Nouns Are Masculine
children.description: Not every noun is masculine; check for feminine markers.
children.exampleTranslation: Sun is feminine, moon is masculine

children.title: Wrong Plural Agreement
children.description: Non-human plurals take feminine singular agreement.

children.title: Confusing Definite and Indefinite
children.description: الـ makes a noun definite; adding Tanween makes it indefinite. Don't use both.

categories.title: Pronouns & Demonstratives
categories.description: Personal pronouns, attached pronouns, demonstratives, relative pronouns, and reflexive forms — the building blocks of Arabic sentences

children.title: Introduction to Pronouns
children.description: Arabic pronouns are either detached (منفصلة) — standing alone as words — or attached (متصلة) — suffixes on verbs, nouns, and prepositions. Understanding them is essential for reading any Arabic sentence.

children.title: Definition
children.description: A pronoun (ضمير) is a word that replaces a noun to avoid repetition. Example: instead of 'Aḥmad went, Aḥmad ate', Arabic says 'Aḥmad went, he ate'.

children.title: Two Main Types
children.description: Detached pronouns stand alone (أَنَا، هُوَ). Attached pronouns are suffixes (ـهُ، ـهَا، ـنَا).

children.title: Detached Personal Pronouns (الضمائر المنفصلة)
children.description: Twelve pronouns covering all persons, genders, and numbers. Used as sentence subjects or emphasis.

children.title: أَنَا (I)
children.description: First person singular, used by both genders.

children.title: نَحْنُ (We)
children.description: First person plural, used by both genders.

children.title: أَنْتُمَا (You — dual)
children.description: Second person dual, used by both genders.

children.title: هُمَا (They — dual)
children.description: Third person dual, used by both genders.

children.title: Attached Pronouns (الضمائر المتصلة)
children.description: Suffixes attached to verbs (as objects), nouns (as possessors), and prepositions (as objects). Same twelve persons but in suffix form.
children.example: ـنِي ـكَ ـهُ ـهَا ـنَا ـكُمْ ـهُمْ

children.title: On Nouns — Possession
children.description: Attached to a noun to show possession. كِتَابِي = my book, كِتَابُكَ = your book, كِتَابُهُ = his book.
children.exampleTranslation: My book / your book / his book

children.title: On Verbs — Direct Object
children.description: Attached to a verb to indicate the direct object. كَتَبَنِي = he wrote me, كَتَبَكَ = he wrote you.

children.title: On Prepositions — Object of Preposition
children.description: Attached to a preposition to indicate its object. لِي = to me, لَكَ = to you, لَهُ = to him.
children.exampleTranslation: To me / to you / to him / to her

children.title: Complete Attached Pronoun Table
children.example: ـنِي، ـنَا، ـكَ، ـكِ، ـكُمَا، ـكُمْ، ـكُنَّ، ـهُ، ـهَا، ـهُمَا، ـهُمْ، ـهُنَّ

children.title: Demonstrative Pronouns (أسماء الإشارة)
children.description: Words meaning 'this' and 'that', with variants for gender, number, and proximity vs distance.

children.title: هَذَا (This — masc. sing.)
children.description: For a nearby masculine singular noun.

children.title: هَذِهِ (This — fem. sing.)
children.description: For a nearby feminine singular noun.

children.title: ذَلِكَ (That — masc. sing.)
children.description: For a distant masculine singular noun.

children.title: تِلْكَ (That — fem. sing.)
children.description: For a distant feminine singular noun.

children.title: هَذَانِ / هَاتَانِ (These two)
children.exampleTranslation: These two books / these two schools

children.title: هَؤُلَاءِ / أُولَئِكَ (These / Those)
children.description: Plural forms for humans (masculine and feminine). For non-human plurals, use feminine singular هَذِهِ / تِلْكَ.
children.exampleTranslation: These are students / those are teachers

children.title: هُنَا / هُنَاكَ (Here / There)
children.exampleTranslation: Here is a book / there is a mosque

children.title: Relative Pronouns (الأسماء الموصولة)
children.description: Words meaning 'who', 'which', 'that' — used to join clauses. They agree with the noun they describe in gender and number.

children.title: الَّذِي (masc. sing.)
children.description: Refers to a masculine singular noun.

children.title: الَّتِي (fem. sing.)
children.description: Refers to a feminine singular noun.

children.title: الَّذِينَ (masc. plural)
children.description: Refers to three or more masculine nouns (usually humans).

children.title: اللَّاتِي / اللَّوَاتِي (fem. plural)
children.description: Refers to three or more feminine nouns.

children.title: Non-Human Plurals Use الَّتِي
children.description: For non-human plural nouns, use feminine singular الَّتِي.

children.title: مَنْ / مَا (Whoever / Whatever)
children.description: Indefinite relative pronouns for humans (مَنْ) and non-humans (مَا).
children.example: مَنْ يَعْمَلْ خَيْرًا / مَا عِنْدَكُمْ يَنْفَدُ
children.exampleTranslation: Whoever does good / whatever you have will run out

children.title: نَفْس (Self)
children.description: Used with attached pronouns: نَفْسِي (myself), نَفْسُكَ (yourself), نَفْسُهُ (himself), etc.

children.title: بَعْض (Some / Each Other)
children.description: With attached pronoun: بَعْضُنَا (some of us), بَعْضُهُمْ (some of them, or each other).

children.title: كُلّ (Each / Every / All)
children.description: With attached pronoun: كُلِّي (all of me), كُلُّنَا (all of us), كُلُّهُمْ (all of them).
children.exampleTranslation: All of you / all of us

children.title: Mixing Gender in Pronouns
children.description: Using هُوَ for feminine nouns or هِيَ for masculine. Each pronoun's gender must match the noun it refers to.
children.exampleTranslation: The sun is she / the moon is he

children.title: Wrong Number Agreement
children.description: Non-human plurals take feminine singular pronouns: الْكُتُبُ هِيَ جَدِيدَةٌ (not هُنَّ).

children.title: Wrong Attachment
children.description: Attached pronouns must attach to the end of the word — verb, noun, or preposition.

categories.title: Verbs — Foundations
categories.description: Past, present, imperative, conjugation, and negation — the heart of Arabic sentences

children.title: Introduction to Arabic Verbs
children.description: Arabic verbs are built from a three-letter root (usually) and conjugate by person, gender, number, and tense. The default verb form is third-person masculine singular past.

children.title: What Is a Verb?
children.description: A verb (فعل) expresses an action or state in time. Arabic verbs come in three tenses: past (ماضٍ), present (مضارع), and imperative (أمر).

children.title: The Root System
children.description: Most Arabic verbs have a 3-letter root. From the root ك-ت-ب come: كَتَبَ (write), كَاتِب (writer), كِتَاب (book), مَكْتَب (office), مَكْتَبَة (library).
children.example: ك ت ب → كَتَبَ، كَاتِب، كِتَاب، مَكْتَب

children.title: Person, Gender, Number
children.description: Verbs conjugate for 3 persons × 2 genders × 3 numbers = many forms. Every verb has a subject embedded in it.
children.exampleTranslation: He wrote / she wrote / they wrote / we wrote

children.title: The Past Tense (الماضي)
children.description: The past tense is the simplest form. You start with the third-person masculine singular (كَتَبَ) and modify the ending for other persons.
children.exampleTranslation: He wrote / she wrote / they wrote

children.title: هُوَ — كَتَبَ
children.description: Third person masculine singular — the base form.

children.title: The Present Tense (المضارع)
children.description: The present tense has a prefix (أ، ت، ي، ن) and a suffix that varies by person. It is used for ongoing and habitual actions.
children.exampleTranslation: He writes / you write / I write / we write

children.title: Mood (الإعراب): Indicative, Subjunctive, Jussive
children.description: Present tense verbs change their ending based on the preceding particle. Default is Indicative (مرفوع) ending in ـُ.
children.exampleTranslation: He writes / he will not write / he did not write

children.title: The Imperative (الأمر)
children.description: Used to command or request. Derived from the present tense by removing the prefix and adjusting the ending.

children.title: Negative Command
children.description: Use لَا + jussive: لَا تَكْتُبْ = Don't write!

children.title: Negation Particles
children.description: Arabic uses different negation particles depending on tense.

children.title: مَا — Negates Past
children.description: مَا كَتَبَ = he did not write.
children.exampleTranslation: He did not write the lesson

children.title: لَا — Negates Present
children.description: لَا يَكْتُبُ = he does not write.
children.exampleTranslation: He does not write the lesson

children.title: لَمْ — Negates Past, Jussive
children.description: لَمْ يَكْتُبْ = he did not write (used with jussive).

children.title: لَنْ — Negates Future, Subjunctive
children.description: لَنْ يَكْتُبَ = he will never write.

children.title: لَيْسَ — Negates Nominal Sentences
children.description: لَيْسَ طَالِبًا = he is not a student.

children.title: مَا ... لَا — Double Negation
children.exampleTranslation: Not what he does not write

children.title: Making Verbs into Questions
children.description: Use interrogative particles to turn statements into questions.

children.title: مَا / مَاذَا — What?
children.description: مَاذَا كَتَبْتَ؟ = What did you write?

children.title: أَيْنَ — Where?
children.description: أَيْنَ كَتَبْتَ؟ = Where did you write?

children.title: مَتَى — When?
children.description: مَتَى كَتَبْتَ؟ = When did you write?

children.title: Most Common Verbs
children.description: Learn these first: كَتَبَ (write), قَرَأَ (read), ذَهَبَ (go), أَكَلَ (eat), شَرِبَ (drink), جَلَسَ (sit), نَامَ (sleep), قَامَ (stand).

categories.title: Verb Patterns (الأوزان)
categories.description: The ten derived verb forms (Awzān) — each form adds a specific meaning to the root

children.title: Introduction to Verb Patterns
children.description: Arabic verbs are built on patterns (أوزان). The 3-letter root (Form I) can be augmented into 9 additional forms (II–X), each carrying a specific shade of meaning.
children.exampleTranslation: Form I, II, III, IV patterns

children.title: What Is a Wazn?
children.description: A Wazn (وزن) is the template pattern of a word. The base template is فَعَلَ (faʿala) — where ف، ع، ل represent the three root letters.

children.title: The Root Template
children.description: Use ف، ع، ل (fāʾ, ʿayn, lām) as placeholders. Root ك-ت-ب in pattern فَعَّلَ → كَتَّبَ.
children.example: ف ع ل → ك ت ب

children.title: The Ten Forms
children.description: Arabic has 10 verb forms. Form I is base; II–X add letters (prefix, doubling, or infix) to modify the meaning.
children.example: I II III IV V VI VII VIII IX X

children.title: Form I (فَعَلَ) — Base Form
children.description: The base pattern with 3 letters. Meaning is usually basic action. Verbs in Form I can have many vowel patterns (فَعَلَ، فَعِلَ، فَعُلَ).

children.title: Common Form I Verbs
children.description: كَتَبَ، قَرَأَ، ذَهَبَ، أَكَلَ، جَلَسَ، نَظَرَ.

children.title: Transitive vs Intransitive
children.description: كَتَبَ is transitive (needs an object); ذَهَبَ is intransitive (no object).
children.exampleTranslation: He wrote the book / he went to school

children.title: Form II (فَعَّلَ) — Intensification / Causation
children.description: Formed by doubling the middle root letter. Usually intensifies the action or makes it causative.
children.exampleTranslation: He knew → he taught / he studied → he taught

children.title: Meaning Shift
children.description: Form II often means 'to cause to do' or 'to make someone/something do': عَلِمَ (he knew) → عَلَّمَ (he taught = made others know).

children.title: Form III (فَاعَلَ) — Mutuality
children.description: Formed by adding Alif after the first root letter. Often indicates action directed toward someone else or reciprocal action.
children.exampleTranslation: He wrote → he corresponded / he killed → he fought

children.title: Mutual / Directed Action
children.description: Form III usually means the action is directed at another: كَاتَبَ (he wrote to someone).

children.title: Form IV (أَفْعَلَ) — Causation
children.description: Formed by adding hamza prefix. Frequently causative.
children.exampleTranslation: He went out → he made go out / he knew → he informed

children.title: Causative Meaning
children.description: خَرَجَ (he exited) → أَخْرَجَ (he brought out / caused to exit).

children.title: Form V (تَفَعَّلَ) — Reflexive of II
children.description: Formed by adding ت prefix to Form II. Often reflexive — the action happens to oneself.

children.title: Reflexive Meaning
children.description: Form V generally makes the action reflect back: عَلَّمَ (he taught) → تَعَلَّمَ (he learned).

children.title: Form VI (تَفَاعَلَ) — Reciprocal
children.description: Formed by adding ت prefix to Form III. Indicates mutual action.
children.exampleTranslation: He helped → they helped each other

children.title: Mutual Action
children.description: Both parties do the action: تَحَاوَرَا (they conversed with each other).

children.title: Form VII (اِنْفَعَلَ) — Passive / Intransitive
children.description: Formed with اِنْ prefix. Usually intransitive and often passive in meaning.
children.exampleTranslation: He broke → it broke / he opened → it opened

children.title: Passive / Reflexive
children.description: Form VII usually means the action happened without specifying the doer: اِنْكَسَرَ الزُّجَاجُ (the glass broke).

children.title: Form VIII (اِفْتَعَلَ) — Reflexive
children.description: Formed by adding اِ and ت. Usually reflexive — the subject does the action to itself.
children.exampleTranslation: He gathered → they gathered / he wrote → he subscribed

children.title: Reflexive Meaning
children.description: Form VIII often means doing the action on oneself or for oneself: اِجْتَمَعَ (they gathered = gathered themselves).

children.title: Form IX (اِفْعَلَّ) — Colors & Defects
children.description: Formed with اِ + doubling of the last letter. Almost exclusively for colors and physical defects.

children.title: Common Form IX Verbs
children.description: اِحْمَرَّ (turn red), اِصْفَرَّ (turn yellow), اِسْوَدَّ (turn black).

children.title: Colors and Physical States
children.description: Reserved for colors (أَحْمَر → اِحْمَرَّ) and physical defects (أَعْوَج → اِعْوَجَّ).

children.title: Form X (اِسْتَفْعَلَ) — Seeking / Requesting
children.description: Formed with اِسْتَ prefix. Usually means 'to seek' or 'to ask for' something.
children.exampleTranslation: He forgave → he sought forgiveness / he extracted

children.title: Seeking / Requesting
children.description: Form X usually means 'to seek X': غَفَرَ (he forgave) → اِسْتَغْفَرَ (he sought forgiveness).
children.exampleTranslation: He sought forgiveness from his Lord

children.title: The Passive Voice (المجهول)
children.description: Passive voice is used when the doer is unknown or unimportant. Formed by vowel change.

children.title: Passive Past — كُتِبَ
children.description: Vowels change to Ḍammah + Kasrah pattern.

children.title: Passive Present — يُكْتَبُ
children.description: Prefix gets Ḍammah, second-to-last gets Fatḥah.

children.title: Derived Nouns from Verbs
children.description: Arabic derives several nouns from a verb root, each with a specific pattern and meaning.

children.title: Active Participle (اسم الفاعل)
children.description: Pattern فَاعِل. Means 'the one who does'. كَاتِب (writer).

children.title: Passive Participle (اسم المفعول)
children.description: Pattern مَفْعُول. Means 'the one done to'. مَكْتُوب (written).

children.title: Verbal Noun (المصدر)
children.description: The noun of the action itself. كِتَابَة (writing).

children.title: Noun of Place (اسم المكان)
children.description: Pattern مَفْعَل or مَفْعِل. مَكْتَب (office/desk), مَكْتَبَة (library).

children.title: Noun of Time (اسم الزمان)
children.description: Also مَفْعَل pattern. Same form as noun of place — distinguished by context. مَوْعِد (appointment).

children.title: Noun of Instrument (اسم الآلة)
children.description: Patterns مِفْعَل، مِفْعَال، مِفْعَلَة. مِفْتَاح (key), مِنْشَار (saw).

categories.title: Weak & Irregular Verbs
categories.description: Verbs that deviate from the standard pattern due to weak letters (و، ي، ا) or hamza

children.title: Introduction to Irregular Verbs
children.description: Arabic verbs are classified as sound (صحيح) if all root letters are strong consonants, or weak (معتل) if one or more root letters is و، ي، or ا. Weak verbs undergo vowel changes and letter drops.
children.exampleTranslation: He said / he sold / he slept

children.title: Sound vs Weak Verbs
children.description: Sound (صحيح): all root letters are consonants. Weak (معتل): one or more root letters is a weak letter (و، ي، ا).

children.title: Assimilated Verbs (المثال)
children.description: First root letter is و or ي. The weak letter often drops.
children.exampleTranslation: He promised → he promises / he arrived → he arrives

children.title: With و — وَعَدَ
children.description: In Form I present tense, the و drops: وَعَدَ → يَعِدُ.

children.title: Hollow Verbs (الأجوف)
children.description: Second root letter is و or ي. In the past tense, the weak letter often changes to ا.
children.exampleTranslation: He said → he says / he sold → he sells

children.title: With و — قَالَ
children.description: Past: قَالَ. Present: يَقُولُ. Imperative: قُلْ.

children.title: With ي — بَاعَ
children.description: Past: بَاعَ. Present: يَبِيعُ. Imperative: بِعْ.

children.title: The Alif in Past
children.description: When the middle weak letter has Fatḥah, it changes to ا in the past: نَامَ (he slept).

children.title: Defective Verbs (الناقص)
children.description: Third root letter is و or ي. Endings vary by person.
children.exampleTranslation: He called → he calls / he forgot → he forgets

children.title: Doubled Verbs (المضعف)
children.description: Second and third root letters are identical. They merge in the past but separate in some forms.
children.exampleTranslation: He extended → he extends / he returned → he returns

children.title: Hamzated Verbs (المهموز)
children.description: Verbs with Hamza in any root position (first, middle, or last).
children.exampleTranslation: He took / he asked / he read

children.title: Quadriliteral Verbs (الرباعي)
children.description: Verbs with 4 root letters instead of 3. Less common but important.

children.title: Form II (تَفَعْلَلَ)
children.description: Reflexive of Form I. تَدَحْرَجَ (it rolled).

children.title: Practice — Reading Irregular Verbs
children.exampleTranslation: Allah said / he was, he is

children.title: قَالَ — Most Common Weak Verb
children.description: Appears over 500 times in the Qur'an.

children.title: كَانَ — The 'To Be' Verb
children.description: Used to form past continuous and other tenses.

categories.title: Particles & Prepositions
categories.description: Prepositions, conjunctions, interrogatives, negation, and emphatic particles — the glue of Arabic sentences

children.title: Introduction to Particles
children.description: Particles (حروف) are function words that carry grammatical meaning but not full lexical meaning on their own. They connect, negate, ask, and modify.
children.example: فِي مِنْ إِلَى لَا هَلْ إِنَّ
children.exampleTranslation: In, from, to, no, do?, indeed

children.title: What Is a Particle?
children.description: A particle (حرف) has no meaning unless attached to another word. It governs how other words behave.
children.example: فِي (in) needs a noun after it: فِي الْبَيْتِ

children.title: Six Categories
children.description: 1. Prepositions (حروف الجر). 2. Conjunctions (حروف العطف). 3. Interrogatives (أدوات الاستفهام). 4. Negation (أدوات النفي). 5. Emphatics (الحروف المشبهة بالفعل). 6. Conditionals (أدوات الشرط).

children.title: Prepositions (حروف الجر)
children.description: Prepositions attach to nouns and put them in the genitive case (الجر). There are 17 classical prepositions.

children.title: فِي (In)
children.exampleTranslation: In the house / in the morning

children.title: مِنْ (From)
children.exampleTranslation: From the school / from the water

children.title: إِلَى (To)
children.exampleTranslation: To the mosque / until the night

children.title: عَلَى (On / Upon)
children.description: Indicates position on top of, or obligation.
children.exampleTranslation: On the table / you must study

children.title: عَنْ (About / From)
children.exampleTranslation: About the lesson / to the right

children.title: كَ (Like / As)
children.exampleTranslation: Like a lion / like the moon

children.title: مُنْذُ / مُذْ (Since)
children.description: Indicates a starting point in time.

children.title: بِ (Extra / Emphatic)
children.exampleTranslation: And Allah is sufficient as a witness

children.title: وَ (And)
children.description: Simple coordination — shares case and meaning.

children.title: أَمْ (Or — in questions)
children.exampleTranslation: Did you write it or he?

children.title: لَكِنْ (But)
children.exampleTranslation: He wrote but he made a mistake

children.title: بَلْ (Rather / But)
children.exampleTranslation: He didn't write, but rather read

children.title: حَتَّى (Even)
children.description: Includes the following as an extreme case.

children.title: كَمْ (How many/much?)
children.exampleTranslation: How many books did you read?

children.title: Negation Particles (أدوات النفي)
children.exampleTranslation: No / not / did not / will not / is not

children.title: لَا (No — present)
children.description: Negates present tense or nominal sentences.

children.title: لَمْ (Did not)
children.description: Negates past with present-tense form, jussive.

children.title: مَا ... مِنْ (Emphatic negation)
children.exampleTranslation: There is no god but Allah

children.title: Emphatic Particles (الحروف المشبهة بالفعل)
children.description: Six particles that resemble verbs in effect — they put the subject in the accusative and predicate in the nominative.
children.example: إِنَّ أَنَّ كَأَنَّ لَيْتَ لَعَلَّ لَكِنَّ
children.exampleTranslation: Indeed / that / as if / would that / perhaps / but

children.title: كَأَنَّ (As if)
children.exampleTranslation: As if he is a lion

children.title: لَيْتَ (Would that / If only)
children.exampleTranslation: Would that the book were with me

children.title: Conditional Particles (أدوات الشرط)
children.description: Particles that introduce a condition — usually followed by two jussive verbs.

children.title: لَوْ (If — hypothetical)
children.exampleTranslation: If you had written, you would have succeeded

categories.title: Sentence Structure
categories.description: Nominal sentences, verbal sentences, and the special particles that modify them

children.title: Introduction to Arabic Sentences
children.description: Arabic has two fundamental sentence types: nominal (جملة اسمية) — beginning with a noun — and verbal (جملة فعلية) — beginning with a verb.
children.exampleTranslation: The house is big / the student writes

children.title: What Is a Sentence?
children.description: A sentence (جملة) is a complete unit of meaning containing at least a subject and predicate or a verb and subject.

children.title: Two Fundamental Types
children.description: Nominal sentences start with a noun. Verbal sentences start with a verb.
children.exampleTranslation: The house is big / the student writes

children.title: Nominal Sentence (الجملة الاسمية)
children.description: Starts with a subject (مبتدأ — Mubtadaʾ) and is followed by a predicate (خبر — Khabar). Both are typically in the nominative case.

children.title: The Subject (المبتدأ)
children.description: The first noun, usually definite, in the nominative case.
children.exampleTranslation: The book is new — 'the book' is the subject

children.title: The Predicate (الخبر)
children.description: The second element, in the nominative case. Can be a noun, adjective, or phrase.
children.exampleTranslation: The book is new — 'new' is the predicate

children.title: Types of Predicate
children.description: 1. Singular noun: الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ. 2. Phrase (prepositional): الْكِتَابُ فِي الْحَقِيبَةِ. 3. Sentence: الْكِتَابُ قَرَأْتُهُ.
children.exampleTranslation: The book is in the bag

children.title: No 'To Be' in Present
children.description: Arabic has no present-tense 'to be'. الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ literally means 'the house big' but translates as 'the house is big'.

children.title: Using كَانَ for Past 'To Be'
children.description: For past tense 'to be', use كَانَ.

children.title: Verbal Sentence (الجملة الفعلية)
children.description: Starts with a verb. Structure: Verb (فعل) + Subject (فاعل) + optional Object (مفعول به).

children.title: The Subject / Doer (الفاعل)
children.description: The doer of the verb, always in the nominative case.

children.title: The Direct Object (المفعول به)
children.description: The thing acted upon, in the accusative case.

children.title: Transitive vs Intransitive
children.description: Transitive verbs need an object (كَتَبَ). Intransitive verbs don't (جَلَسَ).

children.title: Verbs with Two Objects
children.description: Some verbs take two objects: أَعْطَى، أَعْلَمَ، ظَنَّ.
children.exampleTranslation: The teacher gave the student a book

children.title: Attached Object Pronoun
children.description: The object can be an attached pronoun: كَتَبَهُ (he wrote it).

children.title: كَانَ and Its Sisters
children.description: Verbs that put the predicate in the accusative case (نصب).
children.exampleTranslation: Was / became / became (morning) / remained / spent the night

children.title: What Are Kāna and Sisters?
children.description: Verbs of 'being' that modify a nominal sentence by putting the predicate in the accusative case.

children.title: كَانَ (Was/Were)
children.description: The most common — indicates past 'to be'.

children.title: أَصْبَحَ (Became — in the morning)
children.description: Specifically for becoming in the morning.
children.exampleTranslation: The weather became cold (in the morning)

children.title: بَاتَ (Spent the night)
children.exampleTranslation: The soldier spent the night awake

children.title: إِنَّ and Its Sisters
children.description: Emphatic particles that put the subject in the accusative case and predicate in the nominative.
children.example: إِنَّ أَنَّ كَأَنَّ لَكِنَّ لَيْتَ لَعَلَّ
children.exampleTranslation: Indeed / that / as if / but / if only / perhaps

children.title: أَنَّ (That)
children.description: Used mid-sentence after verbs of knowing/saying.
children.exampleTranslation: I knew that Allah is Forgiving

children.title: كَأَنَّ (As if)
children.exampleTranslation: As if the student were a lion

children.title: لَكِنَّ (But)
children.exampleTranslation: The student is smart, but he is lazy

children.title: Negation in Sentences
children.description: How to negate nominal and verbal sentences.
children.exampleTranslation: Not / is not / did not / will not

children.title: Negating with لَيْسَ
children.description: More elegant — لَيْسَ acts like كَانَ.

children.title: Negating Past with مَا
children.description: Insert مَا before the past verb.

children.title: Negating Past with لَمْ
children.exampleTranslation: The student did not write (at all)

children.title: Question Sentences
children.description: How to form questions in Arabic.

children.title: Wh-Questions
children.exampleTranslation: What did you write? / Where is the book?

children.title: Rhetorical Questions
children.description: Common in the Qur'an for emphasis.
children.exampleTranslation: Is not Allah sufficient for His servant?

children.title: Commands & Prohibitions
children.description: How to give commands (imperative) and prohibitions (negative imperative).

children.title: Advanced Sentence Topics
children.description: Fronting, emphasis, and other advanced sentence structures.

children.title: Fronting (التقديم والتأخير)
children.description: Moving an element earlier for emphasis.

children.title: Omission (الحذف)
children.description: Arabic often omits words for brevity.
children.example: قَالَ لِي: اكْتُبْ (meaning قَالَ لِي أَنْ أَكْتُبَ)

children.title: Relative Clauses (الجملة الموصولة)
children.exampleTranslation: The book that I read is new

categories.title: Grammatical Cases (الإعراب)
categories.description: How Arabic words change endings based on their role in the sentence — nominative, accusative, genitive, jussive

children.title: Introduction to Iʿrāb
children.description: Iʿrāb (إعراب) is the system of case endings in Arabic. Every declinable word changes its ending based on its grammatical function.
children.exampleTranslation: The book (nom.) / the book (acc.) / the book (gen.)

children.title: What Is Iʿrāb?
children.description: Iʿrāb means 'declension' — the change of a word's ending to indicate its role. It applies to nouns, adjectives, and present-tense verbs.

children.title: The Three Nominal Cases
children.description: Nouns have three cases: Nominative (رفع), Accusative (نصب), Genitive (جر).

children.title: The Three Verb Moods
children.description: Present-tense verbs have three moods: Indicative (رفع), Subjunctive (نصب), Jussive (جزم).
children.exampleTranslation: He writes / will not write / did not write

children.title: Original vs Substituted Signs
children.description: The default signs are ـُ for nominative, ـَ for accusative, ـِ for genitive, ـْ for jussive. Some words substitute other signs (e.g., dual ـَان / ـَيْن).

children.title: Nominative (المرفوع)
children.description: The default case for the subject and predicate. Original sign: ـُ or ـٌ (Tanween Ḍamm).

children.title: Subject of Verbal Sentence (الفاعل)
children.description: The doer of a verb is nominative.

children.title: Passive Subject (نائب الفاعل)
children.description: In passive voice, the subject is nominative.

children.title: Accusative (المنصوب)
children.description: The case of direct objects and many adverbial meanings. Original sign: ـَ or ـًا (Tanween Fatḥ).

children.title: Circumstantial Accusative (الحال)
children.description: Describes the state of the subject or object at the time of the action.

children.title: Specification (التمييز)
children.exampleTranslation: I have a pound of oil

children.title: Absolute Object (المفعول المطلق)
children.exampleTranslation: I struck him a severe strike

children.title: Object of Reason (المفعول لأجله)
children.exampleTranslation: I stood out of respect for knowledge

children.title: Object of Accompaniment (المفعول معه)
children.exampleTranslation: I walked along with the river

children.title: Adverbial of Time/Place (المفعول فيه)
children.description: Time or place nouns after verbs.

children.title: Genitive (المجرور)
children.description: The case after prepositions and the second term of possessive construction. Original sign: ـِ or ـٍ (Tanween Kasr).
children.exampleTranslation: In the book / the student's book

children.title: After a Preposition (بعد حرف الجر)
children.description: All prepositions make the following noun genitive.
children.exampleTranslation: In the house / from the school

children.title: Second Term of Iḍāfah (المضاف إليه)
children.description: The possessed noun in a possessive construction.

children.title: Partitive Genitive
children.description: مِنْ for part of a whole.

children.title: Jussive (المجزوم)
children.description: Applies only to present-tense verbs. Marks the verb after particles like لَمْ، لَا الناهية، إِنْ الشرطية.
children.exampleTranslation: He did not write / do not write

children.title: Substitute Signs of Iʿrāb
children.description: Some words use substitute signs instead of the original vowels.

children.title: Sound Feminine Plural (جمع مؤنث سالم)
children.description: All cases: ـَات (but nominative has ـَاتٌ with Ḍamm).

children.title: The Five Nouns (الأسماء الخمسة)
children.description: أَب، أَخ، حَم، فُو، ذُو — use ـو، ـا، ـي instead of vowels.

children.title: Sound Verb Endings
children.description: Jussive drops the final vowel or letter.
children.exampleTranslation: He writes → he did not write

children.title: Iʿrāb Practice
children.description: Analyze sentences to identify each word's case.
children.exampleTranslation: The student read the new book

children.title: قَرَأَ الطَّالِبُ الْكِتَابَ
children.description: قَرَأَ: فعل ماضٍ. الطَّالِبُ: فاعل مرفوع. الْكِتَابَ: مفعول به منصوب.

children.title: الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ
children.description: الْبَيْتُ: مبتدأ مرفوع. كَبِيرٌ: خبر مرفوع.

children.title: فِي الْبَيْتِ رَجُلٌ
children.description: فِي: حرف جر. الْبَيْتِ: اسم مجرور. رَجُلٌ: مبتدأ مؤخر مرفوع.

categories.title: Adjectives & Agreement
categories.description: How adjectives work in Arabic — agreement in four aspects, comparatives, colors, and more

children.title: Introduction to Adjectives
children.description: In Arabic, adjectives (نعت / صفة) FOLLOW the noun they describe and agree with it in four aspects: gender, number, case, and definiteness.

children.title: What Is an Adjective?
children.description: An adjective describes a noun's quality. It comes after the noun and follows its grammatical properties.

children.title: Position — After the Noun
children.description: Unlike English, Arabic adjectives always come after the noun.

children.title: The Four Aspects of Agreement
children.description: An adjective must agree with its noun in gender, number, case, and definiteness.

children.title: 1. Gender
children.description: Masculine noun takes masculine adjective; feminine takes feminine.
children.exampleTranslation: Diligent male student / diligent female student

children.title: 2. Number
children.description: Singular, dual, or plural must match.
children.example: طَالِبٌ مُجْتَهِدٌ / طَالِبَانِ مُجْتَهِدَانِ / طُلَّابٌ مُجْتَهِدُونَ

children.title: 3. Case
children.description: Nominative, accusative, or genitive must match.

children.title: 4. Definiteness
children.description: Definite noun takes definite adjective; indefinite takes indefinite.
children.exampleTranslation: The diligent student / a diligent student

children.title: All Four Together
children.description: الطَّالِبَتَانِ الْمُجْتَهِدَتَانِ: feminine, dual, nominative, definite.
children.exampleTranslation: The two diligent female students passed

children.title: Comparative & Superlative (اسم التفضيل)
children.description: Formed on the pattern أَفْعَل. Used for comparisons and superlatives.

children.title: Superlative with ال
children.description: With ال, it means the most.

children.title: Superlative with Iḍāfah
children.description: With possessive, it means the most X of.

children.title: Common Comparatives
children.description: أَكْبَر، أَصْغَر، أَحْسَن، أَفْضَل، أَجْمَل، أَقْرَب، أَبْعَد.

children.title: Colors & Physical Adjectives
children.description: Colors follow a special pattern (أَفْعَل masculine, فَعْلَاء feminine).

children.title: Nisbah Adjectives (النسبة)
children.description: Adjectives formed by adding ـِيّ to a noun. Means 'relating to' or 'of'.

children.title: Rule: Add ـِيّ
children.description: Add ـِيّ (with shaddah) to the noun.

children.title: Countries & Nationalities
children.description: مِصْر → مِصْرِيّ، لُبْنَان → لُبْنَانِيّ، سُورِيَا → سُورِيّ.

categories.title: Numbers & Counting
categories.description: Cardinal and ordinal numbers, agreement rules, and how to count in Arabic

children.title: Introduction to Arabic Numbers
children.description: Arabic numbers follow rules for gender agreement that differ from English. The counting numbers 3–10 take OPPOSITE gender from the noun they count.

children.title: What Are Numbers?
children.description: Numbers (الأعداد) express quantity. Arabic has separate forms for masculine and feminine counted nouns.

children.title: Eastern Arabic Numerals
children.description: Arabic uses its own digit shapes: ٠ ١ ٢ ٣ ٤ ٥ ٦ ٧ ٨ ٩ (0-9). Western digits (0123) are also used in modern contexts.

children.title: Cardinal Numbers 1–10
children.description: Numbers 1–10 with both masculine and feminine forms.

children.title: ١ — وَاحِد / وَاحِدَة
children.description: Placed AFTER the noun as an adjective.
children.exampleTranslation: One male student / one female student

children.title: ٢ — اثْنَان / اثْنَتَان
children.description: The noun is in dual form; the number is often omitted.

children.title: ٣ — ثَلَاثَة / ثَلَاث
children.description: ثلاثة for masculine noun, ثلاث for feminine noun (OPPOSITE gender).

children.title: Cardinal Numbers 11–20
children.description: Numbers 11–19 use the singular noun; 20 uses the plural.

children.title: ١١ — أَحَدَ عَشَرَ
children.description: Both parts masculine; same for feminine أَحَدَةَ عَشْرَةَ.

children.title: ١٣ — ثَلَاثَةَ عَشَرَ
children.description: Both parts match the NOUN's gender (opposite of 3-10 rule).

children.title: Cardinal Numbers Above 20
children.description: Numbers 20–99 use the units followed by tens with وَ (and).

children.title: ١٠٠٠ — أَلْف
children.description: Plural or singular; nouns in genitive.

children.title: Ordinal Numbers
children.description: First, second, third, etc. Follow the pattern فَاعِل for 1-10.

children.title: 11–19 = Cardinal + ال
children.description: Ordinals 11+ use the cardinal form with ال: الْحَادِي عَشَرَ (11th).

children.title: Days of the Week (أيام الأسبوع)
children.description: الْأَحَد (Sun.), الِاثْنَيْن (Mon.), الثُّلَاثَاء (Tue.), الْأَرْبِعَاء (Wed.), الْخَمِيس (Thu.), الْجُمُعَة (Fri.), السَّبْت (Sat.).

children.title: Hijri Months (الأشهر الهجرية)
children.description: مُحَرَّم، صَفَر، رَبِيع الْأَوَّل، رَبِيع الثَّانِي، جُمَادَى الْأُولَى، جُمَادَى الْآخِرَة، رَجَب، شَعْبَان، رَمَضَان، شَوَّال، ذُو الْقَعْدَة، ذُو الْحِجَّة.

children.title: Gregorian Months (الشهور الميلادية)
children.description: يَنَايِر، فِبْرَايِر، مَارِس، أَبْرِيل، مَايُو، يُونْيُو، يُولْيُو، أَغُسْطُس، سِبْتَمْبِر، أُكْتُوبِر، نُوفَمْبِر، دِيسَمْبِر.

children.title: Forgetting Opposite Gender for 3–10
children.description: 3–10 take opposite gender of the counted noun.

children.title: Wrong Case
children.description: Counted noun after 3–10 is genitive plural.

categories.title: Diptotes & Indeclinables
categories.description: Nouns that refuse Tanween (diptotes) and nouns/particles with fixed endings (indeclinables)

children.title: Introduction
children.description: Most Arabic nouns take Tanween and change case endings. Two special groups deviate: diptotes (refuse Tanween in certain cases) and indeclinables (fixed endings).

children.title: What Is a Diptote?
children.description: A noun that takes only two endings (Ḍammah and Fatḥah) instead of three. It never takes Kasrah or Tanween when indefinite.

children.title: What Is an Indeclinable?
children.description: A word with a fixed ending that never changes regardless of grammatical role — mostly pronouns and particles.

children.title: Nine Categories of Diptotes
children.description: Classical grammar identifies nine reasons a noun may refuse Tanween.

children.title: 4. Nouns Ending in ة (with proper reference)
children.description: Any proper noun ending in Tāʾ Marbūṭah.

children.title: How Diptotes Behave
children.description: Diptotes take Ḍammah in nominative and Fatḥah in both accusative and genitive (indefinite).

children.title: When Definite — Take Kasrah Again
children.description: With ال or in Iḍāfah, diptotes behave normally: فِي الْمَسَاجِدِ (with ال), فِي مَسَاجِدِ الْمَدِينَةِ (in Iḍāfah).

children.title: Types of Indeclinables
children.description: Words with fixed endings regardless of grammatical position.

children.title: Personal Pronouns
children.description: هُوَ، هِيَ، أَنْتَ, etc. — fixed endings.

children.title: All Particles
children.description: مِنْ، فِي، إِنَّ, etc. — fixed endings.

children.title: Practice
children.description: Identify diptotes and indeclinables in sentences.

children.title: صَلَّيْتُ فِي مَسَاجِدَ
children.description: مَسَاجِدَ is a diptote — genitive but takes Fatḥah (not Kasrah).

children.title: هَذَا كِتَابٌ
children.description: هَذَا is indeclinable — same form in any case.

children.title: What Is Qur'anic Arabic?
children.description: The register used in the Qur'an — Classical Arabic at its peak, with unique features in style, vocabulary, and syntax.

children.title: Qur'anic vs. Modern Standard

categories.title: Iḍāfah, Tawābiʿ & Advanced Case Topics
categories.description: Possessive construction, adjectives, apposition, coordination, and advanced case usages

children.title: Iḍāfah (الإضافة)
children.description: The possessive construction — linking two nouns where the second possesses the first.

children.title: Definition
children.description: Iḍāfah joins two nouns: the first (المضاف) loses its Tanween and Alif, and the second (المضاف إليه) is in the genitive case.

children.title: The Four Rules
children.description: 1. المضاف loses Tanween and ال. 2. المضاف إليه is genitive. 3. المضاف takes the case of its role in the sentence. 4. The two nouns form one unit.

children.title: Meaning Types
children.description: Iḍāfah can mean possession (كِتَابُ زَيْدٍ), belonging, or attribution (بَابُ الْبَيْتِ).

children.title: Definiteness
children.description: If المضاف إليه is definite, the whole Iḍāfah is definite.
children.exampleTranslation: The student's book / a student's book

children.title: Common Iḍāfah Phrases
children.description: بَيْتُ اللهِ، رَسُولُ اللهِ، يَوْمُ الْجُمُعَةِ، أَهْلُ الْكِتَابِ.

children.title: The Four Tawābiʿ (التوابع)
children.description: Four types of words that follow a preceding noun and match it in case: النعت، البدل، العطف، التوكيد.

children.title: Four Types
children.description: 1. Naʿt (adjective). 2. Badal (apposition). 3. ʿAṭf (coordination). 4. Tawkīd (emphasis). All follow the case of the preceding noun.

children.title: Naʿt (النعت) — Adjective
children.description: Describes a preceding noun, agreeing with it in gender, number, case, and definiteness.

children.title: Four Agreements
children.description: Agrees in: gender, number, case, definiteness.

children.title: Two Types: Ḥaqīqī and Sababī
children.description: Ḥaqīqī describes the noun directly. Sababī describes something related to the noun.
children.exampleTranslation: The useful book / the student whose brother is diligent

children.title: Badal (البدل) — Apposition
children.description: A word that substitutes for or clarifies the preceding noun.

children.title: Three Types
children.description: 1. Badal Kullī (identical). 2. Badal Baʿḍ (part of). 3. Badal Ishtimālī (related).

children.title: Kullī (Complete Substitution)
children.description: The بدل is identical to the preceding.

children.title: Baʿḍ (Part of the Whole)
children.description: The بدل is part of the whole.
children.exampleTranslation: I ate the loaf, a third of it

children.title: Ishtimālī (Related)
children.description: The بدل is a related attribute.

children.title: ʿAṭf (العطف) — Coordination
children.description: Joining two nouns with a conjunction. The second takes the case of the first.

children.title: Nine Conjunctions
children.description: وَ، فَ، ثُمَّ، أَوْ، أَمْ، بَلْ، لَكِنْ، حَتَّى، لَا.

children.title: Example
children.exampleTranslation: The student and the teacher came

children.title: Tawkīd (التوكيد) — Emphasis
children.description: Reinforcing a preceding noun. Two types: lafẓī (verbal) and maʿnawī (semantic).

children.title: Maʿnawī — Words of Emphasis
children.description: Uses نَفْس، عَيْن، كِلَا، كِلْتَا، كُلّ، جَمِيع، عَامَّة.

children.title: Object of Reason (المفعول لأجله)
children.exampleTranslation: I stood out of respect for knowledge

children.title: Object of Accompaniment (المفعول معه)
children.exampleTranslation: I walked along with the river

children.title: Specification (التمييز)
children.exampleTranslation: I have a pound of oil

children.title: Special Constructions
children.description: Unique Arabic constructions for emphasis, praise, warning, and exclamation.

children.title: Praise (نِعْمَ)
children.description: نِعْمَ الْعَبْدُ = Excellent is the servant.

children.title: Blame (بِئْسَ)
children.description: بِئْسَ الْعَمَلُ = How bad is the deed.

categories.title: Classical vs. Modern Arabic
categories.description: How Arabic has evolved — the registers, dialects, and differences between Qur'anic/Classical Arabic and Modern Standard Arabic

children.title: Introduction to Arabic Registers
children.description: Arabic exists in multiple registers. Understanding them explains why the Qur'an sounds different from a newspaper.

children.title: What Is a Register?
children.description: A register is a variety of language used in a particular context. Arabic has three main registers: Classical, Modern Standard, and Dialectal.

children.title: Classical Arabic (الفصحى التراثية)
children.description: The Arabic of the Qur'an, Hadith, and classical literature. Preserved unchanged for over 1400 years.
children.exampleTranslation: And Muhammad is but a messenger

children.title: Definition
children.description: The language of pre-Islamic poetry, the Qur'an, and early Islamic texts. Fully inflected with case endings, dual forms, and classical vocabulary.

children.title: Key Features
children.description: Full Iʿrāb, classical word order, rich vocabulary, no borrowed words, use of dual, use of energetic mood (نون التوكيد).

children.title: Modern Standard Arabic (الفصحى المعاصرة)
children.description: The standardized form used in news, literature, education, and formal writing across the Arab world today.
children.exampleTranslation: The government announced a new plan

children.title: Definition
children.description: Descended from Classical Arabic but simplified in style. Used for writing across the Arab world; spoken only in formal contexts.

children.title: Key Features
children.description: Simplified Iʿrāb in casual writing, borrowed words (تِلِفِزْيُون، حَاسُوب), modern constructions, avoidance of rare classical forms.

children.title: Differences from Classical
children.description: Simpler sentence structure, less Iʿrāb in practice, more borrowed vocabulary, some dialectal influence in idioms.

children.title: Dialects (العامية)
children.description: Regional spoken varieties that differ significantly from both Classical and Modern Standard Arabic.

children.title: Egyptian Arabic (المصرية)
children.description: Most widely understood due to Egyptian media. Uses hard 'g' for ج, drops final vowels.

children.title: Levantine Arabic (الشامية)
children.description: Spoken in Lebanon, Syria, Jordan, Palestine. Uses 'sh' for negation.

children.title: Gulf Arabic (الخليجية)
children.description: Spoken in Gulf states. Uses distinctive vocabulary.

children.title: Maghrebi Arabic (المغربية)
children.description: Spoken in Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia. Heavily influenced by French and Berber.

children.title: Learn MSA/Classical First
children.description: Understanding Fusha unlocks the Qur'an, news, and literature. Dialects are easier to learn afterward.

children.title: Pick a Dialect for Speaking
children.description: Choose based on where you'll travel or work. Egyptian for broad understanding; Levantine for the Middle East.

children.title: Both Together
children.description: Many learners study Fusha formally and absorb a dialect from daily exposure.

categories.title: Writing, Orthography & Rhetoric
categories.description: Arabic script rules, spelling conventions, and the classical science of eloquence (Balāghah)

children.title: Introduction to Arabic Writing
children.description: Arabic is written right-to-left using a cursive script. Understanding spelling conventions (Imlāʾ) is essential for correct writing.

children.title: Direction: Right to Left
children.description: Arabic is written and read from right to left. Numbers are written left to right within an Arabic sentence.

children.title: Cursive Script
children.description: Letters within a word usually connect, forming a continuous flow.

children.title: Two Orders
children.description: 1. Modern: أ ب ت ث... 2. Abjad (historical): أ ب ج د...
children.example: أ ب ت / أ ب ج

children.title: Hamza Writing Rules (رسم الهمزة)
children.description: Rules for when Hamza sits on Alif, Wāw, or Yāʾ, or stands alone.
children.example: أ إ آ ؤ ئ ء

children.title: Middle Hamza — Based on Vowels
children.description: Rule: compare the vowel before and after; the stronger vowel wins (Kasrah > Ḍammah > Fatḥah).
children.example: سُئِلَ (on Yāʾ because Kasrah wins) / مُؤْمِن (on Wāw because Ḍammah wins)

children.title: Standalone Hamza (ء)
children.description: Used after long vowels or Sākinah letters.

children.title: Alif Writing Rules (رسم الألف)
children.description: When to write or omit the Alif.

children.title: Alif Written
children.description: Default — Alif is written when pronounced.

children.title: Alif Omitted
children.description: In some words like الرَّحْمَٰن (Raḥmān written with dagger Alif instead).

children.title: Tāʾ Marbūṭah Rules (التاء المربوطة)
children.description: When to write ة vs. ه vs. ت.

children.title: When to Use ة
children.description: Feminine nouns and adjectives. Pronounced 'h' at pause, 't' in construction.

children.title: When to Use ه
children.description: Regular letter H, or attached pronoun 'his/him'.

children.title: When to Use ت
children.description: Open Tāʾ appears in some feminine nouns and verbs.

children.title: Punctuation in Arabic
children.description: Modern Arabic uses punctuation marks similar to Western conventions but with Arabic-specific forms.

children.title: Arabic Comma (،)
children.description: Inverted comma — same function as English.

children.title: Arabic Semicolon (؛)
children.exampleTranslation: I read the book; then I returned it

children.title: Colon (:)
children.exampleTranslation: He said: I am the servant of Allah

children.title: Introduction to Balāghah (البلاغة)
children.description: Balāghah is the science of eloquence. It has three branches: ʿIlm al-Maʿānī، ʿIlm al-Bayān، ʿIlm al-Badīʿ.

children.title: What Is Balāghah?
children.description: The art of conveying meaning in the most effective way, appropriate to the situation. Foundational to understanding Qur'anic inimitability.
children.exampleTranslation: Eloquence is matching speech to context

children.title: Three Branches
children.description: 1. ʿIlm al-Maʿānī (syntax of meaning). 2. ʿIlm al-Bayān (figures of speech). 3. ʿIlm al-Badīʿ (embellishments).

children.title: ʿIlm al-Bayān (Figures of Speech)
children.description: The science of metaphor, simile, and figurative language.

children.title: Tashbīh (التشبيه) — Simile
children.description: Comparison using كَ or similar words. Example: زَيْدٌ كَالْأَسَدِ (Zayd is like a lion).

children.title: Istiʿārah (الاستعارة) — Metaphor
children.description: Comparison without the comparative word. Example: رَأَيْتُ أَسَدًا يَخْطُبُ (I saw a lion giving a speech).

children.title: Kināyah (الكناية) — Metonymy
children.description: Indirect expression. Example: فُلَانٌ كَثِيرُ الرَّمَادِ (so-and-so has much ash — meaning: very generous).

children.title: Majāz (المجاز) — Figurative Speech
children.description: Using a word beyond its literal meaning.
children.example: جَرَى الْمَاءُ فِي النَّهْرِ (literal) / جَرَى الْحَدِيثُ (figurative)
children.exampleTranslation: The water ran / the conversation ran

children.title: Jinās (الجناس) — Paronomasia
children.description: Similar-sounding words with different meanings. Example: الْخَيْلُ وَالْخَيْلُ (horses and horses).
children.exampleTranslation: Woe to every slanderer and backbiter

children.title: Ṭibāq (الطباق) — Antithesis
children.description: Pairing opposites. Example: وَتَحْسَبُهُمْ أَيْقَاظًا وَهُمْ رُقُودٌ.
children.exampleTranslation: You would think them awake while they were asleep

children.title: Muqābalah (المقابلة) — Contrast
children.example: فَأَمَّا مَنْ أَعْطَى وَاتَّقَى... وَأَمَّا مَنْ بَخِلَ وَاسْتَغْنَى
children.exampleTranslation: As for one who gives and fears Allah... but as for one who withholds and is self-sufficient

children.title: Taṣdīr (التصدير) — Repetition at Start and End
children.description: Repeating a word at the start and end of a phrase.
children.example: لَا تَرَى فِيهَا عِوَجًا وَلَا أَمْتًا
children.exampleTranslation: You will not see therein any crookedness or deviation

children.title: Rhetoric Practice — Qur'anic Examples
children.description: Analyze Qur'anic verses for rhetorical devices.

children.title: Sūrah Al-ʿAṣr (103:1-3)
children.description: Uses oaths (القسم), antithesis, and rhymed prose.
children.exampleTranslation: By time, indeed mankind is in loss

children.title: Sūrah Al-Kawthar (108:1)
children.exampleTranslation: Indeed We have given you al-Kawthar

children.title: Sūrah Al-Ikhlāṣ (112:1-4)
children.exampleTranslation: Say: He is Allah, the One
